title: Pope Leo XIV Declares Family the 'First School of Humanity' in Sweeping AI Encyclical
excerpt: The pontiff's 83-page teaching document 'Magnifica Humanitas' calls for an educational alliance to protect human dignity in the age of artificial intelligence.
body:
• Pope Leo XIV's first encyclical, "Magnifica Humanitas," is an 83-page document calling for the protection of human dignity in the age of artificial intelligence.
  • The pontiff describes family as "the first school of humanity" and urges an "educational alliance for the digital age" to safeguard children from technology's harms.
  • The document demands that AI be "disarmed" — stripped of military and economic exploitation — and subjected to stricter international regulation.
  • Anthropic co-founder Chris Olah joined Vatican officials at the encyclical's presentation, calling on religious communities and civil society to push AI development "in a better direction."

A Papal Warning on Technology's Reach

Pope Leo XIV has issued the most comprehensive moral framework on artificial intelligence ever produced by the Catholic Church, warning in his first encyclical that AI risks widening inequality, weakening democracy and eroding what it means to be human.

The 83-page teaching document, titled "Magnifica Humanitas" (Magnificent Humanity), was presented at the Vatican's Synod Hall on May 25 alongside high-ranking prelates, theologians, and Chris Olah, co-founder of the American AI company Anthropic. It frames artificial intelligence as the defining challenge of a new industrial revolution and makes an urgent appeal to "disarm" the technology.

"Disarming AI means freeing it from the mentality of 'armed' competition, which today is not limited simply to the military context, but is also an economic and cognitive phenomenon."

— Pope Leo XIV, Magnifica Humanitas

"Disarming does not mean renouncing technology, but preventing it from dominating humanity," Leo wrote. "For this reason, merely regulating it is insufficient; it must be disarmed, welcoming and accessible."

Family as the First Classroom

At the heart of the encyclical is Leo's insistence that families, schools and policymakers forge what he calls an "educational alliance for the digital age." The pope describes the family as the first school of humanity — a place where values, empathy and critical thinking are transmitted before any algorithm can intervene.

"Rapid technological transformations reveal just how unprepared we are on the educational level," Leo wrote, arguing that the "pervasiveness of digital media" fosters "a culture of immediacy and hyper-stimulation" that gives rise to "fatigue, boredom and apathy concerning the effort required for seeking the truth."

Luke Rowe, a lecturer at the Australian Catholic University, said the guidance moved him deeply. "I think I didn't realize how much I was longing to hear this guidance," he told OSV News. "And I think the world needs it right now."

The pope urged educators not to abandon a generation that could be "lost to technology," describing education as "a long journey requiring patience" that needs "time for development and for engagement with reality beyond appearances."

Big Tech Under Scrutiny

Leo took direct aim at the concentration of technological power, warning that "AI tends to amplify the power of those who already possess economic resources, expertise and access to data." Small but influential groups, he wrote, "can shape information and consumption patterns, influence democratic processes and steer economic dynamics to their own advantage."

The encyclical pushes back against Silicon Valley philosophies of transhumanism and posthumanism that interpret progress as "surpassing the human condition." Leo argued that "humanity flourishes not despite limitations, but often through them."

In a nod to companies like Anthropic that have adopted ethical AI constitutions, the pope cautioned that such frameworks must still be subjected to broader social scrutiny. "A more moral AI is not enough if that morality is determined by a few," he wrote.

Olah, speaking at the Vatican event, acknowledged that AI development "operates inside a set of incentives and constraints that can sometimes conflict with doing the right thing." He called on religious communities, civil society, scholars and governments to "take this seriously, to look closely, and to push events in a better direction."

What Comes Next

The document builds on a decade of dialogue between the Vatican and the tech industry and draws on Catholic social teaching dating back to Pope Leo XIII's 1891 encyclical "Rerum Novarum," which addressed the challenges of the first industrial revolution.

"I feel entrusted to oversee another great transformation through the eyes of faith, with the clarity of reason, and with openness to the divine mystery," Leo said at the presentation.

Brian Patrick Green, director of technology ethics at Santa Clara University's Markkula Center for Applied Ethics, called the encyclical "a landmark opportunity for the world to look at a new technology and really think about what it is for."

The pope also addressed the military use of AI, calling for "the most rigorous ethical constraints" and insisting that responsibility for lethal action remain with human beings, not machines. He called for international laws to govern the growing use of automated weapons.

The encyclical has already drawn strong endorsement from Catholic leaders and technology ethicists worldwide, positioning the Vatican as one of the most prominent institutional voices demanding accountability from the AI industry.
nri_angle: The encyclical's call for AI regulation and its emphasis on family-centered education resonate with Indian diaspora parents navigating their children's growing dependence on digital technology.
